newsitem.title: FRANCE: FORECAST - French franc seen steady until 1999.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - French franc seen steady until 1999.

text.p: The French franc is expected to be at 3.38 per mark, unchanged from current levels, on the eve of a planned move to a single European currency in January 1999, a Reuter poll published on Thursday showed.
The median forecast of the 10 financial institutions gave a prediction for the fourth-quarter 1998 of 3.38 per mark, with forecasts ranging from 3.35 to 3.55.
Only three of the 10 institutions expected the franc to be at 3.35 per mark, its central pivot rate in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
The Bank of France has repeatedly held that the correct rate for the franc against the mark is the pivot rate.
European authorities have yet to decide the exact procedure and at what rates individual European currencies will be converted into a single Euro currency.
But officials are looking at using either ERM pivot rates or an average of rates over a given period to fix exchange rates at the start of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
As in the previous Reuters quarterly survey, a forecast by HSBC James Capel, whose economists predicted a rate of 3.55 per mark, stood out from the herd.
Stephen King, economist at HSBC James Capel said the forecast was based on the premise EMU would be delayed.

The poll also showed economists expected the franc to remain stable throughout the coming two years. The highest median forecast was for 3.3850 per mark in the third quarter of 1997 and the second quarter of 1998. The median forecast in every other quarter was 3.3800.
Economists expected the Bank of France's key intervention rate, now at 3.25 percent, to continue declining slightly in coming quarters before starting to pick up again towards the end of 1998.
DKB International was the only institution to forecast a sizeable reduction in the key French interest rate, predicting a rate of two percent in the first quarter of 1997.

Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB in London, said the forecast was based on the view that sluggishness in the French economy, combined with a stable franc, would allow the Bank of France to take short-term rates well below those in Germany.
Economists also predicted the spread, or risk premium, between 10-year French and German bond yields would remain stable to the end of 1998.
Of the nine institutions that gave a forecast for the fourth quarter of 1998, six said the spread would be zero. Based on its outlook for short-term rates, DKB said it would be minus 20 basis points.

So far this year, the spread has steadily narrowed from a high of 67 on January 8 to minus five basis points on Thursday, helped by growing conviction monetary union will take place and there will be strong domestic demand for French bonds.
The poll, conducted between October 16 and October 22, was part of a quarterly survey of French indicators, interest rates and exchange rates.
